title: Calibration and few guesses
summary: Do your numbers match real life, and why a handful of guesses proves little.

steps.head: Do your numbers match life?
steps.body: {{calibration|Calibration}} asks a simple thing. Of the times you said 70%, did about 7 in 10 go up?

steps.head: Putting guesses in groups
steps.body: We group your guesses by size, such as 60 to 70%. Then we compare each group with what really happened.

steps.head: Too sure
steps.body: Say your 90% guesses went up only 6 times in 10. You were too sure. This is called {{overconfidence|overconfidence}}.
steps.more: Most people start out too sure. Seeing it in your own numbers is the first step to fixing it.

steps.head: Few guesses prove little
steps.body: A group of five guesses can look perfect or awful by chance alone. You need many guesses in a group before you can trust it.

steps.head: What to do with this
steps.body: Keep guessing and look first at the groups with the most guesses. Do not change your style after a few misses.

questions.prompt: Your 80% guesses went up 5 times in 10. What does this suggest?

options.why: Yes. If you say 80%, about 8 in 10 should go up. 5 in 10 means your number was too high.
No. Just right would be about 8 in 10.
No. Too careful would mean more than 8 in 10 went up.

questions.prompt: Why do five guesses in a group prove little?

options.text: Chance alone can give almost any result.
options.why: Right. With so few guesses, a lucky or unlucky run is common.
No. More guesses make a group more reliable, not fewer.
No. Small groups can look perfect or awful. That is the problem.

questions.prompt: Which group of guesses should you trust the most?

options.text: The group with the most guesses.
options.why: Right. More guesses means less room for luck to fool you.

options.text: The group with the fewest guesses.
options.why: No. A few guesses can be lucky.
No. How much you like a result says nothing about how reliable it is.
